analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal health insurance program, modeled on the one Congress members get, covering everyone who lacks other coverage.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2004 with zero cosponsors, sent to two House committees, and died without a hearing or vote when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would enroll every U.S. resident not already covered by Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, the VA, or Indian Health Service into a private health plan chosen from a menu like the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program. The government would pay roughly 72-75% of the premium, low-income families would get premiums and out-of-pocket costs wiped out, and insurers could no longer reject people or charge more for being sick. It would be financed by a new 6% tax on employers' payrolls and a 6% tax on self-employment income.
analysis.who_benefits: The uninsured (43.6 million in 2002, 80% of them workers or their dependents, per the bill's own findings) would get comprehensive coverage they cannot lose by changing jobs. People below about 125-150% of the poverty line, children, and pregnant women would pay nothing in deductibles or copays, and premium subsidies would phase out only above twice that income level. People with pre-existing conditions would be guaranteed coverage at the same community-rated price as everyone else.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an American Health Benefits Program covering all U.S. citizens, permanent residents, refugees, and certain long-term residents who lack Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, VA, or Indian Health Service coverage, with plans contracted like the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program.

Qualified health plans must cover the full FEHBP benefit scope, cannot exclude or discriminate based on pre-existing conditions or genetic information, and must use community-rated premiums that do not vary by age, gender, or health status.

The government contributes up to 75% of the premium (computed as 72% of the regional weighted average), and people below 125% of poverty (individuals) or 150% (families), plus all children and pregnant women below the cost-sharing threshold, owe zero cost-sharing.
Anyone who fails to enroll is automatically assigned to a plan with a below-average premium, so coverage does not lapse through inaction.
States would get a boosted federal Medicaid matching rate for services to program-eligible people, while the separate SCHIP children's program sunsets once the new program starts.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new 6% excise tax on all wages, and self-employed people a 6% tax on their income, with the proceeds funding the program. Enrollees would pay the remaining premium share (roughly 25-28%) through payroll withholding or direct payment, though low-income households would get most or all of it back through subsidies. Workers may ultimately bear part of the employer tax through slower wage growth.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, the self-employed, and enrollees' premium shares

drawbacks.text: The financing is a new 6% payroll tax on every employer and 6% tax on self-employment income, a substantial permanent cost that economists generally expect to be partly passed to workers through wages.
Coverage is mandatory: every eligible person must enroll, and anyone who does not choose a plan is defaulted into one, a requirement that was politically contested in this era.

The program has no public insurance option; all coverage flows through contracts with private insurers, who become the permanent gatekeepers and are compensated for subsidies and risk by the government.

The bill sunsets SCHIP funding entirely once the program takes effect, so states that run strong children's coverage programs would lose that federal money and depend on the new federal program working as designed.
The bill contained no cost estimate or funding analysis beyond a directive for Comptroller General studies, and it was never vetted by a committee hearing or markup.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is enormous and concrete: universal coverage with strong consumer protections, zero out-of-pocket costs for the poorest families, and coverage tied to the plan Members of Congress get rather than to employment. The costs are also real: a broad new 6% tax on employment, mandatory enrollment with default assignment, and a design that permanently routes public money through private insurers rather than creating a public alternative. The biggest weakness is that the bill was a single-sponsor sketch — no cosponsors, no cost scoring, no committee review — so its fiscal soundness was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and their Health subcommittees in July 2004, and with no cosponsors and no further action, it expired when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. James Langevin introduced the bill on July 22, 2004, late in the second session of the 108th Congress, with introductory remarks in the Congressional Record.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and then to the Health subcommittees in early August 2004.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, killing the bill under the rule that legislation does not carry over between Congresses.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and self-employed people were better off because the bill died, since it would have imposed a new 6% tax on their payroll and income. Health insurers kept the status quo, which also meant no new regulation of their underwriting or premiums. The 43.6 million uninsured gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided the new payroll tax

sides.party_line_note: One Democrat sponsored the bill and no one from either party cosponsored it, so no vote ever revealed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would make private insurers the permanent channel for universal coverage: the government contracts with licensed insurers for FEHBP-style plans, pays up to 75% of premiums, reimburses them for cost-sharing subsidies, and reinsures their high-cost patients. Insurers gain a guaranteed national customer base, while giving up pre-existing condition exclusions and medical underwriting.

A new 6% excise tax on all wages would replace (for most workers) employers' role in buying insurance, but employers currently covering workers would pay the tax on top. The bill's findings argue it stabilizes business costs, which were rising about 14% a year.
The bill's findings cite $35 billion a year in uncompensated care for the uninsured; universal coverage would convert much of that bad debt into paid claims.
States would lose all federal SCHIP funding when the program starts, but would receive a higher federal Medicaid matching rate (40% of the gap to 100%) for services to program-eligible people.
